item.title: (Why) we’re launching the next cohort of Generator
item.description:
Published on October 14, 2026 5:41 AM GMT

TL;DR: The first round of the Generator Residency went very well.

Our residents created and ran several large-scale fieldbuilding, talent infrastructure, and operational projects that have already had important impacts on the ecosystem.  

Six weeks after the program ended, 12 of our 27 residents have been hired to full-time roles at core AI safety orgs, and most have received several offers. 

Kairos and Constellation are running a second round from January to April 2027. Apply to the next round of the Generator Residency by November 1st. 

Introduction

In April, we wrote AI Safety's Biggest Talent Gap Isn't Researchers. It's Generalists. 

We wrote this because we noticed that organizations across the ecosystem were struggling to hire for key non-research roles. While these roles were often getting many applicants, candidates didn’t meet basic requirements.

The original memo we wrote (that became the post above) inspired us to create the Generator Residency as an intervention to support more generalists trying to break into AI safety.

The program concluded six weeks ago, and this post details the successes we’ve seen from the first round of Generator, which have inspired us to launch a second round of the program.     

Programs and projects from Generator

Programs residents started:

  • Talent Commons, a cross-organization talent directory now run as a Kairos product, which will include data from participants in SPAR, Pathfinder, GCP, Generator, BlueDot courses, Astra, Anthropic Fellows, OpenAI Safety Fellows, and MATS.
  • Praxis, a retreat bringing top national debaters into contact with AI safety: about 40 debaters, including 20 national champions.
  • Lateral, a three-day workshop bringing mid-career professionals to Berkeley to work with AI safety professionals: 705 applications for about 35 seats, and a likelihood to recommend of 9.7 out of 10 from attendees.
  • Gen Stream, a one-week program in London funded through Generator.
  • Longitude DC, an eight-day policy intensive for 15 early-to-mid-career technical AI safety professionals with more than 20 speakers, running October 6 to 13.
  • M3, an AI security matching fellowship, which raised $200k from BlueDot on top of Generator funding.

Residents working with mentors at established organizations contributed to:

  • Lab engagement through Nightingale and Constellation.
  • Recruiting and strategy at METR.
  • A frontier robotics benchmark program for Robocurve.
  • Events at Constellation.
  • Fundraising and hiring for a new organization founded by Jeff Alstott.
  • The Plan A launch, in collaboration with AI Futures Project.
  • Founder scouting for Coefficient Giving's Project Tailwind.

Other notable projects included:

  • A one-week AI safety world-modeling bootcamp with 25 attendees covering ML fundamentals, futurism, and the technical case for alignment.
  • A workshop series on improving management within AI safety (interviews with more than 10 managers and three workshops).
  • AI safety founder support (meetings with 32 founders, with 6 given deeper support).
  • Support for mid-career operations people transitioning into AI safety (leading to hundreds of referrals across more than 50 roles).
  • A map of the work on AI character and model specs.
  • 12 SPAR generalist projects that came out of the residency.

Resident Outcomes 

Generator was designed as a path into full-time generalist roles in AI safety. Six weeks after the program ended, 12 of the 27 residents have been hired into full-time positions. Their employers include BlueDot Impact, Guidelight, Constellation, Kairos, METR, Eleos, CBAI, and CEA. In several of these cases, the hiring organization began working with the resident during Generator. 

Of the residents who have not yet taken a full-time role, some are running programs that came out of the residency or AI safety university groups at Harvard, Princeton, MIT, and Stanford. Others have received offers, including from Coefficient Giving, Quorum, and ARENA, and are deciding between options. A few residents have been pitched by funders on turning their one-time project into a much larger, recurring program. 

Below are a couple of selected testimonials from previous residents: 

Additional testimonials and information are available on the Generator website.

Reflections

We stood Generator up in three months. It was the first multi-month in-person program Kairos had run. Most of what we learned was about what residents needed from us, and we think most of it applies to other programs that support people rather than research outputs. 

Some key lessons we learned: 

1. Candidate selection shaped the program more than anything else. 

Candidate selection is, of course, an incredibly important part of any program. However, we were surprised by just how much of our planned programming changed based on the proactivity of our participants. 

Residents discovered who the other residents were before the program started and created a group chat and had calls with each other. Once they arrived, they ran hikes, game nights, regular reflection sessions, and informal peer check-ins. When we asked what made them feel integrated, residents pointed to these resident-run activities far more often than anything we scheduled. In both our midway and final surveys, the most common answer to “what was your favorite part” was the other residents.

2. Residents' career goals strongly informed their preferences for projects and advisors. 

The cohort included three broad groups:

  • University organizers looking for their first formal work experience
  • Early-career professionals looking for a final stepping stone into the field
  • Mid-career professionals looking for the context they needed to transition

Over time, we realized that, in addition to accommodating residents with different experience levels, we needed to accommodate residents with different intentions for how Generator could forward their career. Some residents strongly preferred to use the Generator residency to explore multiple roles, while others were using the residency to deliver a legible product that could help them make a career transition or get hired. Residents aiming to transition wanted advisors invested in their growth and career, not only in the project. 

Based on feedback, we’ve decided to implement two tracks in our next residency. We plan to work with our residents from the start to determine what projects and tracks best suit their goals.

3. Our residents asked for the most support with project scoping, structured management, and navigating interpersonal conflict. 

For many residents, their Generator project was the largest or most complex project they had ever planned. Moreover, their projects typically aimed to address large, poorly defined problems in the AI safety ecosystem, such as mid-career talent pipelines. Accordingly, they wanted support in determining the most ambitious, yet feasible project that could enable their vision. 

Several early-career residents benefited from structured management, reporting that they grew from an advisor who had them estimate how long each planned task would take or a short written template before each check-in. 

Co-leading a Generator project was quite similar to co-founding, which led to a lot of interpersonal work for some residents who had previously mostly worked independently. These residents benefitted from clear norms around sharing feedback. 

4. We need to be more explicit that we're betting on people, not projects.

While many residents worked on impactful projects, the main focus of Generator was always on the people we chose to support. The projects matter, and many of them helped the field, but we mostly saw them as a way for residents to grow quickly into the generalists AI safety needs. We didn't say this clearly enough at the start, and many residents felt stressed about picking the single most impactful project. 

When we asked them how the program changed their thinking, the most common answers were about learning field context, clarifying their career direction, and developing self-knowledge. Few people directly mentioned their project outcomes.

Generator 2.0

We’ve been really happy with the outcomes that we saw from the first round of Generator and, as a result, have decided to run a second round! 

Applications for the winter 2027 Generator Residency open on October 12, 2026, and close at the end of the day on November 1, 2026, Anywhere on Earth. The program begins on January 18 and will run until April 9, 2027, with a possible 3-month extension. 

Learn more and apply here

Residents at Generator receive $8,500 per month and are funded for travel to and from Berkeley. Once they arrive in Berkeley, they work from Constellation, are paired with experienced advisors from the AI safety ecosystem, and are offered budgets to pursue their projects.

Applicants do not need to be U.S. citizens. For most international applicants, we can sponsor a J-1 visa for the program’s duration, though we cannot guarantee obtaining one. Additionally, we strongly recommend that international applicants apply early (ideally by October 26th) so we can meet deadlines for visa applications.

item.title: ML4Good Impact Assessment
item.description:
Published on October 15, 2026 10:43 AM GMT

Summary

ML4Good bootcamps from 2022-2025 have successfully achieved our objectives of getting more people working in AI safety. 

  • An estimated 186 alumni are now working in AI Safety in some capacity (~55% of all participants), or the equivalent of 147 FTE.
  • Many of these participants consider our bootcamp the main reason they're currently working in AI safety. Based on self-reported counterfactuals, we estimate that around 77 of those 147 FTE would not have happened without ML4Good.
  • Several alumni-founded communities have been developed as a direct result of ML4Good.
  • We receive strongly positive feedback from all of our bootcamps, and 98% of participants recommend ML4Good.[1]
  • There are many caveats and uncertainties, especially around how we attempt to measure counterfactual impact, so we want to be transparent about this

How we've done this

At ML4Good, we run annual follow-up surveys to keep track of what people are doing and to measure our impact. 

In late 2025, we sent our alumni survey to 340 alumni, 223 of whom responded. Of those, 135 are now doing something in AI safety, adding up to about 98 full-time equivalents (FTE). 

After estimating outcomes for the people who didn't reply, we think that around 186 of the 340 (~55%) are doing something in AI safety, or ~147 FTE. Based on what alumni told us about ML4Good's counterfactual impact, we estimate that ~77 FTE were counterfactual - these people would not be spending their time on AI safety absent ML4Good.  Like others in the field, we find counterfactual impact hard to measure, so we're less confident in this figure than in the others. We also have over 200 recent alumni from 2026 bootcamps that we haven't yet followed up with. 

We’re reporting all of our costs for the evaluation period openly, and we make an estimate of how cost-effectively we get people into AI Safety work. We calculated a “fully-loaded” cost of £5.4k per FTE, or £9.3k per counterfactual FTE produced.

We’re publishing our data and letting other field-builders know our best guess at how many people are working in AI safety as a result of ML4Good, and at what cost. We’ll also give some caveats and uncertainties about our results, and a bottom line estimate of our impact, given all considerations.

Summary of activities

As of October 2026, there will have been 31 ML4Good bootcamps across 12 countries since August 2022. Over this period, we’ve trained around 600 alumni. 

We initially focused on technical bootcamps. After becoming an organisation in early 2025, we scaled up our operations to run 9 bootcamps last year, and developed a new Governance & Strategy curriculum, before scaling to 12 a year in 2026. 

We've operated in the highlighted countries.

What this impact assessment covers

Our impact assessment covers 17 bootcamps (340 participants), including 13 from Europe (inc. UK), 3 in Latin America, and 1 in Asia. 

We haven’t yet run our latest round of alumni surveys, therefore only our bootcamps up until the end of September 2025 were included in this analysis. All except one were technical bootcamps. It also doesn’t include two bootcamps run in 2023 with SafeAI Lausanne in Switzerland, which used slightly differing surveying strategies.

Community building as an indirect result of ML4Good has also caused many more people to engage with or contribute to AI safety. However, we don’t have concrete numbers on this and chose not to include this in our evaluation.

What we aim for

ML4Good plays a role fairly high up the funnel in the AI safety talent pipeline. Our focus is on providing a transition point for people thinking seriously about a move into AI Safety. We're relatively selective - in 2026, we accepted around 15% of applicants. We usually target people who have engaged with entry level content, such as BlueDot, online technical safety courses, or reading the relevant literature, e.g. LessWrong/EA forum/80,000 Hours content, but who have usually not yet committed to a concrete path[2]. 

After ML4Good, we encourage and support alumni to take future steps to contribute to AI safety. Some alumni start targeted research programmes like MATS, Pivotal, SPAR, ERA, and Talos. Others enter direct roles in AI Safety, conduct independent work, or found new organisations. Some find ways to integrate AI safety into their current work, which can be promising, particularly for our alumni working in policy and law. 

Over 8 days, we create a motivating in-person environment where participants are guided by inspiring teachers and surrounded by other participants with similar goals. We aim to empower attendees to think ambitiously about how to have an impact, to act with high agency, and to find whereabouts in AI safety they are best suited to contribute. They spend the final days of the bootcamp making and starting to implement concrete plans.

While most of our bootcamps run in Europe, we have also succeeded in identifying and supporting talented people across five continents, often in areas with limited AI safety ecosystems. Our strongest outcomes are in Europe, where many of our alumni have gone on to form important parts of the AI Safety ecosystem. Our earlier bootcamps mostly attracted people with technical backgrounds, but, with our expansion beyond technical programmes, we’re now broadening our reach to people from diverse professional backgrounds, and generalists.

Outcomes

To track outcomes, we send follow-up surveys to alumni. We aim to survey people about 6 months after their bootcamp and then once a year after that.[3] 

This survey data gives us a picture of what our alumni are working on. We use this primarily as evidence to adjust our approaches – to see where things are going well and to check whether our bootcamps are having the intended impact. 

We ask what difference the bootcamp made to them, what actions they took as a direct result of the bootcamps, what they’ve been up to since, what they’re doing now, further AI Safety programmes they’ve done (e.g. MATS, ARENA), and the counterfactual impact that ML4Good has had. See the survey here for our specific questions.

From our last surveys in August and November 2025, we had a 66% response rate (223 of 340 participants). 

To see whether the profiles of responders and non-responders would differ significantly, we tracked non-respondent outcomes via LinkedIn for 3 bootcamps to assess whether non-respondents are less likely to engage in AI Safety post-bootcamp. Non-respondents had a very slightly lower engagement in AI safety on average.

We then extrapolated from this estimate with a correction factor applied to estimate outcomes for all 340 participants. Our full methodology, including how we scored FTE and counterfactual impact, and how we extrapolated to non-respondents, is in Appendix 2. 

The table below illustrates what people are doing after ML4Good. We’re very confident in the baseline figures for how many ML4Good alumni are doing something in AI Safety. Our confidence is lower for both counterfactual impact and extrapolated information for non-respondents. 

Participant outcomes span a range of roles and engagement levels. This is the distribution of reported positions from respondents:

  • 55 were pursuing further AI safety programmes, including MATS, ARENA, SPAR, LASR, Talos, Pivotal, MARS, ERA, ARBOx, AI Safety Camp and GovAI fellowships, at the time of surveying. This is the most common next step for participants.
  • 14 in direct technical AI safety roles
    • Alumni mention roles at Timaeus, the London Initiative for Safe AI, and independent work funded by Coefficient Giving.
  • 15 in direct governance roles
    • Positions include the EU AI Office, CeSIA[5], the Observatorio de Riesgos Catastróficos Globales, and GovAI
  • 6 in AI safety entrepreneurship
    • Our alumni have had founding roles at several major European AI Safety orgs
  • 7 doing PhDs in AI safety, and an additional 13 have written or are writing PhD or Masters theses on AI safety topics
  • 10 in independent AI safety research
  • 17 in professional field-building[6], 25 in voluntary fieldbuilding (e.g. running university groups)
    • At least 12 AI safety communities have been founded by alumni, including:
      • Buenos Aires AI Safety Hub, Argentina’s first AI safety community, founded in July 2024.
        • 350+ community members, 15-person volunteer leadership team, 6 full-time AI Safety roles
        • Runs official BlueDot Technical AI Safety cohorts
        • AISAR research fellowship: 6 scholars, 3 ICLR workshop papers
        • Developing MATSx Buenos Aires with Ryan Kidd advising
      • AI Safety Saarland - launched October 2025 with a 300+ attendee event featuring an Anthropic safety team speaker.
        • Runs two fellowships: intro course (30 participants) and research incubator (14 mentors, 33 mentees)
        • Holds regular public events including an Apart def/acc hackathon hub (50 attendees)
        • Has ~100 regularly engaged members within three months
        • Founder has joined with Safe AI Germany to scale the incubator nationally
      • AI Safety Bulgaria, AI Safety Mexico, AI Safety Colombia, Lisbon AI Safety Hub

There were no obvious patterns as to whether people doing more ambitious things attributed more or less of their impact to our bootcamps. 

Several of our highly successful alumni attribute an over-95% counterfactual impact to ML4Good. To cherry-pick a few exceptional examples, this category includes an early alumnus who is now an AI security researcher at a Paris-based AI policy organisation, an AI governance fellow at a European think tank, the founder of a highly successful field-building programme in Germany, and someone building the technical infrastructure for model evals with the EU AI Office.

A much higher number (89 alumni) report an over-50% counterfactual impact. These include a 2024 alumnus who took part in a research fellowship, led a nine-month independent project and is now a control researcher at a leading AI safety organisation, a 2025 alumnus moving into a technical role at an EU body that enforces rules on the algorithms and AI systems used by large platforms, and a research manager at MATS.

As well as these career changes, our alumni generally give positive qualitative feedback about the bootcamps and how ML4Good has impacted their careers. Some of these answers strongly indicate counterfactual impact, such as mentioning targeting roles or fellowships that they applied for during the bootcamp, or as a direct consequence of ML4Good.

As well as nudging people towards working in AI safety, it also helped some people already committed to AI Safety to refine their plans, clarify their theory of change, or try something more ambitious. For example, some realised that they were a better fit for non-technical or founding work.

Negative responses were rare. Out of 206 people who answered these questions, 8 alumni mentioned downsides - feeling more burned out, overwhelmed or more anxious about AI risks. 2 people mentioned that ML4Good made them realise that AI safety wasn't a good fit for them. 11 alumni mentioned applying for things that they didn't get into, and 6 mentioned that they would have taken similar actions without the camp.

Differences between bootcamps

Our bootcamps all follow a similar structure and curriculum, but there is variation in terms of teachers, participants, location, and timing. There are many different variables, so it's difficult to come to strong conclusions about what works and what doesn't. 

In terms of direct FTE working in AI safety, our strongest outcomes so far have been in Europe. This is probably for two reasons:

  1. Europe’s relatively mature AI safety ecosystem gives alumni clear pathways into roles; and
  2. The underlying pool of people exposed to AI safety ideas is a lot larger than the other regions we’ve covered, so we’ve been able to select slightly stronger participants

The data from Latin America shows fewer direct career transitions, but our bootcamps there have driven strong community-building outcomes, including the founding of AI Safety hubs in Argentina, Colombia and Mexico, which have in turn attracted new people to AI safety. In newer communities, alumni often have to build the path first by starting groups, making connections, and securing funding. Many of the people now working on AI safety in Latin America have a connection to our bootcamps, either as alumni or through the hubs alumni founded. There is also far less AI Safety activity in Latin America, meaning that more of our impact is likely to be counterfactual. 

All things considered, while we opted not to do any in 2026, our bootcamps in Latin America were promising enough to merit further bootcamps in the region in 2027.

We collected survey data on Singapore very soon after the bootcamp in 2025; although a few people had already made career transitions directly, and attributed some of this to ML4Good, we expect that this year’s follow-up survey will capture more accurate data.

We ran bootcamps in Canada and South Africa earlier in 2026, and will run one in Hong Kong in late October 2026. Survey data from these bootcamps will inform whether we intend to go to different countries and regions next year. 

Cost-effectiveness

We’ve always taken cost-effectiveness very seriously, and, from our 2025 estimates, our bootcamps run at roughly £1,850 ($2440) per participant, including overhead and off-season costs. 

For context, EAGx events, which are shorter, non-residential, and not designed to provide active training, cost around £430 ($570) per attendee; EA Globals cost £630–£1,855 ($834-$2460) per person. While we don’t have much information about the running costs of other field-building programmes in AI safety, ML4Good bootcamps run more cheaply than most long-term residential fellowships that provide accommodation in urban centres, salaries, and significant compute costs. 

£473,55387 FTE≈£5,443 per FTE

£473,55351 counterfactual FTE≈£9,285 per counterfactual FTE

A naive extrapolation of our cost-effectiveness looks like £5.4k per FTE, or £9.3k per counterfactual FTE produced, calculated from £473,553 spent across bootcamps covered by previous funding, divided by 87 FTE and 51 counterfactual FTE from those specific bootcamps.

Caveats

We want to be very open about our uncertainties. 

Is “more people working in AI Safety” the right metric?

The FTE scoring is not a standardised metric, and is only meant as a proxy for meaningful AI safety work. There are a few reasons that this might not be the ideal metric:

  • It counts all work equally. The impact of people working full-time on entry-level fellowships is not directly comparable to those who have founded or run orgs. An attempt to quantify would probably find that founding a major org in the AI safety ecosystem is orders of magnitude more impactful than someone joining a research fellowship. Even within research fellowships or organisations being founded, some of these are more likely to reduce existential and catastrophic risk than others. We initially tried to score what people were doing on this axis, but we decided it would add too many arbitrary decisions to the model.
  • Not all AI Safety work is clearly positive. Although we do not appear to have any alumni working for frontier labs, or on dangerous capabilities, some of our alumni may be doing AI Safety research that is making AI-related catastrophic harm more likely.
  • It’s timing-sensitive. Our metric only captures a snapshot of whether people are spending their time on AI safety at the time of response, and not whether they are working in stable full-time work. Over multiple years "Is working on AI safety at any given time" becomes a good proxy for full-time work, but less so for a single snapshot a few months after a bootcamp.
  • Goodhart's law says that when a metric becomes a target, it stops being a good metric. Counterfactual FTE metrics are still only a proxy for reduction of catastrophic and existential risk. We don't optimise hard for these metrics, so this doesn't seem a significant risk, but it could reduce trust from skeptical observers.

Overall, we do think this metric captures what we want to do in a way that allows us to compare across bootcamps. We expect that the impact of our alumni is non-linear, and this heavy tail is less well captured by our quantitative metrics. For this reason, we also look at our alumni qualitatively.

Shouldn’t we have more rigorous counterfactuals?

Laura Thomas-Walters’ piece on “Do AI Safety Talent Programmes Work? Nobody has run the study that would tell us” correctly notes that AI Safety Talent Programmes haven’t been great at determining counterfactual impact, or at least reporting this impact publicly. We also haven’t met the gold standard for determining counterfactual impact with either random or quasi-random methods.

Appendix 2: Impact Assessment Methodology

To estimate the impact of ML4Good bootcamps on participants' careers in AI safety, we used follow-up surveys, combined with some manual research on LinkedIn, and extrapolated our survey results for non-respondents. This is a brief overview of how we did this:

Surveys

We sent two rounds of follow-up surveys to bootcamp alumni. The first, in August 2025, covered bootcamps up to March 2025. In the second, as well as this qualitative question, respondents were asked to put a number from 0 to 1 on the counterfactual impact of attending. 

Scoring

For each survey response, we assigned two scores on a scale from 0 to 1:

  • Full-time equivalent (FTE) score: a rough measure of how much of the person's working time is now spent on AI safety–related work. For instance, someone running a successful university AI safety group part-time might score 0.2, someone working full-time in a technical AI safety role would score closer to 1.     • Full-time programmes or full-time AI safety roles: 1
    • Field-building:
      • Running a group: 0.1
      • Running a more involved group/Pathfinder fellowship: 0.2
      • Running a national group/very active group: 0.3
      • Thesis change:
        • Undergraduate: 0.4
        • Masters: 0.6
        • PhD: 1
  • Counterfactual score: a measure of how much of that involvement is attributable to ML4Good specifically. For the first survey round (without a numerical self-reported counterfactual question), this was estimated by the assessor based on the participant's written description. For the second round, we used the participant's self-reported score, adjusting it only where the assessor judged it to be clearly over- or understated.

We then multiplied these two scores to produce a counterfactual FTE figure for each respondent, asking: "how much full-time AI safety work is this person doing as a direct result of ML4Good?"

We also tagged each respondent with categories describing their activities since the bootcamp (e.g. "further programme", "voluntary field-building", "technical research"), and flagged individuals who are currently upskilling or preparing for future roles, to distinguish them from those with no engagement at all.

Extrapolation to non-respondents

We expected that survey respondents are likely to be more engaged in AI safety than non-respondents, so extrapolating raw survey results would overestimate our overall impact. To correct for this, we manually researched non-respondents from three bootcamps (via LinkedIn) and scored them using the same criteria. We then calculated the ratio of non-respondent scores to respondent scores at those three bootcamps, and averaged these ratios.

We applied these ratios to estimate contributions from non-respondents for each of the remaining bootcamps, using the formula:

Extrapolated FTE total for bootcamp A = Bootcamp A total FTE from survey + (Bootcamp A total FTE from survey ÷ number of respondents) x Ratio x Number of non-respondents

These were calculated per-bootcamp then summed to get the total extrapolated FTE.

For counterfactual FTE, we calculated the ratio of counterfactual FTE to FTE among respondents (0.53 across all bootcamps) and applied it to the extrapolated FTE total.

There are a few additional caveats with this process:

  • Not all non-respondents keep their public profiles up to date, so the manual research on non-respondents is likely an underestimate, especially of non-full-time work.
  • Non-responders may be likely to attribute less of their success to ML4Good. We didn't have a way to account for this.

Summary

ML4Good bootcamps from 2022-2025 have successfully achieved our objectives of getting more people working in AI safety. 

  • An estimated 186 alumni are now working in AI Safety in some capacity (~55% of all participants), or the equivalent of 147 FTE.
  • Many of these participants consider our bootcamp the main reason they're currently working in AI safety. Based on self-reported counterfactuals, we estimate that around 77 of those 147 FTE would not have happened without ML4Good.
  • Several alumni-founded communities have been developed as a direct result of ML4Good.
  • We receive strongly positive feedback from all of our bootcamps, and 98% of participants recommend ML4Good.[1]
  • There are many caveats and uncertainties, especially around how we attempt to measure counterfactual impact, so we want to be transparent about this

How we've done this

At ML4Good, we run annual follow-up surveys to keep track of what people are doing and to measure our impact. 

In late 2025, we sent our alumni survey to 340 alumni, 223 of whom responded. Of those, 135 are now doing something in AI safety, adding up to about 98 full-time equivalents (FTE). 

After estimating outcomes for the people who didn't reply, we think that around 186 of the 340 (~55%) are doing something in AI safety, or ~147 FTE. Based on what alumni told us about ML4Good's counterfactual impact, we estimate that ~77 FTE were counterfactual - these people would not be spending their time on AI safety absent ML4Good.  Like others in the field, we find counterfactual impact hard to measure, so we're less confident in this figure than in the others. We also have over 200 recent alumni from 2026 bootcamps that we haven't yet followed up with. 

We’re reporting all of our costs for the evaluation period openly, and we make an estimate of how cost-effectively we get people into AI Safety work. We calculated a “fully-loaded” cost of £5.4k per FTE, or £9.3k per counterfactual FTE produced.

We’re publishing our data and letting other field-builders know our best guess at how many people are working in AI safety as a result of ML4Good, and at what cost. We’ll also give some caveats and uncertainties about our results, and a bottom line estimate of our impact, given all considerations.

Summary of activities

As of October 2026, there will have been 31 ML4Good bootcamps across 12 countries since August 2022. Over this period, we’ve trained around 600 alumni. 

We initially focused on technical bootcamps. After becoming an organisation in early 2025, we scaled up our operations to run 9 bootcamps last year, and developed a new Governance & Strategy curriculum, before scaling to 12 a year in 2026. 

We've operated in the highlighted countries.

What this impact assessment covers

Our impact assessment covers 17 bootcamps (340 participants), including 13 from Europe (inc. UK), 3 in Latin America, and 1 in Asia. 

We haven’t yet run our latest round of alumni surveys, therefore only our bootcamps up until the end of September 2025 were included in this analysis. All except one were technical bootcamps. It also doesn’t include two bootcamps run in 2023 with SafeAI Lausanne in Switzerland, which used slightly differing surveying strategies.

Community building as an indirect result of ML4Good has also caused many more people to engage with or contribute to AI safety. However, we don’t have concrete numbers on this and chose not to include this in our evaluation.

What we aim for

ML4Good plays a role fairly high up the funnel in the AI safety talent pipeline. Our focus is on providing a transition point for people thinking seriously about a move into AI Safety. We're relatively selective - in 2026, we accepted around 15% of applicants. We usually target people who have engaged with entry level content, such as BlueDot, online technical safety courses, or reading the relevant literature, e.g. LessWrong/EA forum/80,000 Hours content, but who have usually not yet committed to a concrete path[2]. 

After ML4Good, we encourage and support alumni to take future steps to contribute to AI safety. Some alumni start targeted research programmes like MATS, Pivotal, SPAR, ERA, and Talos. Others enter direct roles in AI Safety, conduct independent work, or found new organisations. Some find ways to integrate AI safety into their current work, which can be promising, particularly for our alumni working in policy and law. 

Over 8 days, we create a motivating in-person environment where participants are guided by inspiring teachers and surrounded by other participants with similar goals. We aim to empower attendees to think ambitiously about how to have an impact, to act with high agency, and to find whereabouts in AI safety they are best suited to contribute. They spend the final days of the bootcamp making and starting to implement concrete plans.

While most of our bootcamps run in Europe, we have also succeeded in identifying and supporting talented people across five continents, often in areas with limited AI safety ecosystems. Our strongest outcomes are in Europe, where many of our alumni have gone on to form important parts of the AI Safety ecosystem. Our earlier bootcamps mostly attracted people with technical backgrounds, but, with our expansion beyond technical programmes, we’re now broadening our reach to people from diverse professional backgrounds, and generalists.

To track outcomes, we send follow-up surveys to alumni. We aim to survey people about 6 months after their bootcamp and then once a year after that.[3] 

This survey data gives us a picture of what our alumni are working on. We use this primarily as evidence to adjust our approaches – to see where things are going well and to check whether our bootcamps are having the intended impact. 

We ask what difference the bootcamp made to them, what actions they took as a direct result of the bootcamps, what they’ve been up to since, what they’re doing now, further AI Safety programmes they’ve done (e.g. MATS, ARENA), and the counterfactual impact that ML4Good has had. See the survey here for our specific questions.

From our last surveys in August and November 2025, we had a 66% response rate (223 of 340 participants).

Non-respondents had a very slightly lower engagement in AI safety on average.

We are sharing this update partly to report back on what that support has helped build, and partly because we would value funding, advice, collaboration, introductions and interest from people who may want to work with Sanku.

Introduction

Sanku has grown roughly tenfold in three years while reducing the amount of philanthropy required per person reached. In 2023, we were helping millers fortify flour consumed by around 7 million people. Today, we estimate that around 70 million people consume flour fortified through Sanku-supported mills across Tanzania, Kenya and Ethiopia. Sanku is also now beginning work in Uganda, our fourth country, where operations are just getting underway. Net donor cost per person has fallen over the same period from $0.55 to around $0.10 per year.

Sanku has also changed considerably since many people in the EA community may have last encountered it. Our early Sanku model focused primarily on reaching small and medium mills that conventional large-scale fortification systems often missed. The Dosifier we invented to address that problem remains core to our work, but Sanku now works with mills of all sizes and has built local nutrient manufacturing, supply chains, field operations, quality systems, commercial revenue streams and government partnerships around the technology.

The EA community and people influenced by its ideas helped Sanku reach this stage. Sanku began as an initiative within Project Healthy Children (PHC), which was recognised by GiveWell as a Standout Charity from 2016 to 2021, when GiveWell retired the category. Sanku remains recommended by The Life You Can Save. We wanted to share what that support has helped build, what we have learned from scaling across Tanzania, Kenya and Ethiopia, and where we think the next opportunities and uncertainties lie.

The timing also feels relevant to two current discussions in global health and EA: food fortification and absorptive capacity. GiveWell is actively exploring large-scale food fortification opportunities in Africa and has described the intervention as the most promising category within its current anaemia-control search.[2] At the same time, recent discussion in global health and in EA has focused on whether organisations with promising interventions also have the leadership, systems, recruitment capacity and concrete plans required to deploy substantially more funding well.[3] Both questions are directly relevant to where Sanku is now.

Why fortification can be highly cost-effective

Food fortification is widely regarded as one of the most cost-effective nutrition interventions available. WHO describes it as such such, and the broader evidence base supports fortification as an effective way to address several important micronutrient deficiencies when the right food vehicle reaches the target population and fortification is delivered consistently.[4]

Part of the advantage is that fortification can build on staple-food production and distribution channels that already reach very large populations. Micronutrients can be added during normal food processing and then consumed repeatedly through foods people already buy and eat, generally requiring little behaviour change from consumers. The nutrient inputs themselves are relatively inexpensive, and production, quality-assurance and monitoring costs can be spread across large volumes. Importantly, however, this does not mean the infrastructure required for fortification already exists or works well everywhere.

By adding essential vitamins and minerals during food processing, fortification can reduce anaemia, neural tube defects and other health consequences of micronutrient deficiency. Sanku formulates its premix to meet national fortification standards, so the nutrient mix varies by country and can include iron, zinc, vitamin A, folic acid and other B vitamins. Ethiopia’s national standard notably excludes iron, so Sanku’s Ethiopian premix does too.

Where fortification falls short in practice

Fortification policy often runs ahead of effective implementation. Many countries have mandatory standards, but that does not mean all flour is fortified, or fortified consistently to the required standard. Small and medium mills may lack dosing equipment, affordable and reliable premix, packaging, training and technical support. Larger mills generally have more capacity, but can still face problems with premix quality, testing, supply reliability, monitoring, enforcement and compliance.

The implementation gap is also economic. Fortification adds costs for millers, while consumers often have limited willingness or ability to pay more for fortified flour than for an otherwise similar unfortified product. A model that depends only on requiring mills to absorb those costs can therefore be difficult to sustain, particularly in competitive and fragmented markets. Effective fortification needs to address the commercial incentives alongside the technical and regulatory constraints.

From a small-mill technology to a broader fortification system

Sanku was created to address a persistent gap in existing fortification systems: reaching the small and medium mills that many families rely on for their staple flour. Conventional fortification programmes have generally been better suited to large industrial producers, leaving many smaller mills without the equipment, affordable premix, training and support needed to fortify consistently. Sanku’s early work focused on making fortification practical in those mills.

Sanku invented the Dosifier to make fortification practical in these smaller mills. The Dosifier is a patented, IoT-enabled machine fitted directly to milling equipment, with nearly 1,800 units now deployed. It automatically adds a precise amount of nutrient premix as flour is produced and can transmit operating data through a cellular connection, allowing Sanku to monitor use remotely and identify when a mill needs maintenance, restocking or support.

One of our earliest scaling lessons was that the technology was only one part of making fortification work reliably. Working directly with millers made clear that consistent fortification also depended on reliable premix supply, training, maintenance, quality assurance, field support and an enabling regulatory environment. Sanku gradually built these capabilities around the Dosifier, including supply chains, field teams, monitoring systems, commercial operations and government partnerships.

Building local nutrient premix production was one of the most important additions to Sanku’s model. Sanku built and operates Eastern Africa’s first dedicated nutrient premix factory in Tanzania, which opened in 2024. Before this, millers depended heavily on imported premix, with high costs, long lead times and greater supply risk. Local production has significantly reduced costs and lead times while giving Sanku greater control over quality and supply. A second factory in Addis Ababa has now been completed and premix production will officially start in November this year.

Sanku now works across the milling sector, from last-mile village mills to large producers. The small and medium mills Sanku was created to reach remain central to the model, but larger producers can reach millions of people and use the same nutrient-production, supply-chain and quality assurance (QA) infrastructure. Working across the sector has contributed substantially to Sanku’s recent growth and commercial revenue.

Working with larger mills also makes additionality harder to estimate. At many small mills, RP assumes fortification without Sanku is negligible. Large mills are more likely to fortify to some degree anyway, and the available evidence on what would happen without Sanku is limited. Our reach figure therefore measures the number of people estimated to consume flour fortified through Sanku-supported systems; it is not itself a measure of counterfactual impact. We return to this below because improving the evidence on this question is now one of our priorities.

Three lessons from scaling across Tanzania, Kenya and Ethiopia

Scaling across Tanzania, Kenya and Ethiopia has given us a clearer view of what it takes to grow effectively. Three lessons in particular are shaping our next phase.

1. Build with millers, and adapt to the market

Working directly with millers has shaped both our technology and our wider operating model. More than 500 millers were involved in the R&D and field testing of the Dosifier, providing feedback based on real operating conditions. In Tanzania, millers told us that reducing what they spent on flour bags would make it easier to absorb the cost of fortification. Sanku now produces and sells millions of bags each month, with the commercial margin helping offset the cost of premix.

Local market conditions also shape which parts of the model work in each country. We initially expected the bag model to work in Kenya too, but it did not prove viable there. It is currently used only in Tanzania, although we think it may be well suited to Uganda. Our approach is therefore to take the underlying capabilities — technology, nutrient production, QA, monitoring, supply chains and field operations — into new countries while adapting how they are deployed locally.

2. Establish stronger baselines before entering new markets

Stronger baseline data should improve both how we design new-country work and how credibly we estimate its additional impact. In Kenya and Ethiopia, we did not establish as strong a baseline before scaling as we would now want, which makes it harder to estimate retrospectively what would have happened without Sanku. This is particularly important when working with larger mills, where some fortification may already be happening. Before entering new markets, we now want a clearer picture of existing fortification and compliance, the structure of the milling sector and the main implementation gaps. The RP work discussed below reinforced the importance of doing this earlier.

3. Recruitment and People Ops can become a constraint on scale

Our experience aligns with two recent arguments about absorptive capacity: Jack Lewars’s Donors should push animal welfare and global health charities to have more robust scaling plans and Berke Çelik and Tony Senanayake’s People Operations Gap in Global Health. Both argue, in different ways, that scaling effectively requires investing in management, recruitment and people systems before they become bottlenecks.

As Sanku expanded from one country to three, recruitment and People Ops sometimes constrained how quickly we could build the teams we needed. Limited funding certainty has also sometimes made it harder to recruit continuously and move quickly when particularly strong candidates became available. For the next phase, we want to invest more now in recruitment and People Ops, alongside leadership and other enabling functions, so that we can hire, develop and retain the people needed to scale effectively.

What we learned from the Rethink Priorities analysis — and how we’re acting on it

Alongside what we had learned from scaling, we wanted an independent cost-effectiveness analysis to identify where our current work could improve, understand the most important evidence gaps and uncertainties, and better inform future country expansion. We therefore commissioned and funded Rethink Priorities (RP) to analyse our work in Tanzania, Kenya and Ethiopia. RP is responsible for the report and its conclusions. The full report is available here.

RP estimates substantial differences in impact and cost-effectiveness across the three countries covered by the analysis. It reports its cost-per-DALY estimates both gross of revenue and net of revenue; in the net figures, revenue from Sanku’s commercial sales is used to offset programme costs.

RP’s multiple of GiveWell’s benchmark combines its modelled health and economic benefits. See the full report for the methodology and assumptions.

The difference between the gross and net figures also shows the role of Sanku’s commercial model: revenue from miller sales reduces the philanthropic cost of generating a given level of modelled impact. All else equal, as commercial revenue covers a larger share of operating costs over time, the net-of-revenue cost per DALY should fall further.

Part of the difference across countries reflects the maturity and scale of Sanku’s operations. RP says Tanzania’s stronger result reflects “both the maturity and scale of the Tanzanian operation” as well as its relatively low-compliance environment. Tanzania is our oldest and largest operation, while Kenya and Ethiopia are newer markets that have not yet reached the same scale. RP’s cost analysis also finds that fixed country-presence costs are particularly important at low operating scale. These factors are only part of the explanation, however; country context and counterfactual assumptions also have a major effect on the results.

Tanzania has the strongest results. RP estimates Tanzania at ~4.6× GiveWell’s benchmark today, which it describes as “commendably close” to GiveWell’s current 6× funding bar. It estimates ~8.2× if all Sanku-supported flour in Tanzania switched to using the iron compound NaFeEDTA, which would put Tanzania above that bar. We plan to make the switch only for our small maize mills, and subject to securing the necessary funding, so the full 8.2× should be read as an upper bound rather than an estimate of the planned transition.

Kenya and Ethiopia score lower for different reasons. In Kenya, much of Sanku’s work is with industrial-scale mills, which RP assumes would already fortify to some degree without Sanku. That assumed counterfactual fortification comes with substantial uncertainty, and RP says cost-effectiveness would be significantly higher under plausible alternative values. RP also models a higher-counterfactual scenario in which these estimates fall substantially. In Ethiopia, the national fortification standard excludes iron. Iron accounts for more than 90% of the DALYs RP estimates Sanku averts in Tanzania and Kenya, and all of RP’s modelled economic-benefit channels are linked to iron. Ethiopia therefore has no modelled wage gains. At the same time, commercial revenue reduces Ethiopia’s estimated cost per DALY from $1,918 gross to $617 net of revenue, and RP notes that its revenue model may be particularly sustainable.

There is substantial uncertainty around the estimates, and RP notes that its assumptions may “either upwardly or downwardly bias our headline results”. It identifies three particularly important uncertainties: counterfactual fortification, the estimated effects of fortification on relative risks for key health outcomes, and the assumption of a linear dose-response relationship between nutrient intake and health impacts.

For example, one potential upward bias is the assumption that any additional malaria risk from increased iron intake is negligible. RP notes that the evidence is mixed and cites a 2026 Cochrane review finding little to no effect of iron supplementation on clinical malaria overall. Given the relatively low malaria prevalence in the three countries analysed, RP does not model this effect, but notes that this may slightly overstate estimated health benefits. In the other direction, the report excludes possible indirect effects from Sanku’s work on fortification among non-partner mills, which may bias its estimate of total benefits downwards.

How we’re acting on the findings

  • Switching Tanzania’s small maize mills back to NaFeEDTA, subject to funding. The iron compound we use today fully meets Tanzania’s national fortification standard and continues to deliver meaningful health benefits. But RP’s analysis finds that switching to the more bioavailable NaFeEDTA could increase those benefits substantially and improve cost-effectiveness. We used NaFeEDTA previously and stepped back from it following stockouts, logistical challenges and cost pressures. We are targeting small maize mills because maize’s higher phytate content makes the benefit of the more bioavailable iron compound particularly important there, and because the switch is operationally feasible for these mills; large wheat mills are not currently a practical target. Subject to securing funding for the additional cost, we plan to make the switch.
  • Improving baseline data before entering new markets. As discussed above, we want a clearer picture of existing fortification and compliance before scaling, particularly where larger mills may already be fortifying to some degree but the quality and consistency of that fortification are uncertain. This should help us design around the actual implementation gaps and estimate our counterfactual impact more credibly, while also giving us a better basis for assessing any indirect impact on fortification beyond Sanku partner mills.
  • Sharpening how cost-effectiveness informs expansion decisions. Cost-effectiveness is already an important input into how we assess opportunities to scale. The RP analysis gives us a stronger basis for using it alongside evidence, operational feasibility and country context when deciding where and how to expand.

Why scale further, and what it will take

Micronutrient deficiencies remain a major global health burden, while many countries still lack the infrastructure and systems needed to fortify staple foods reliably at scale. Uganda is now Sanku’s fourth country, with operations just getting underway. Over roughly the next decade, we aim to grow to around ten countries and reach approximately one billion people annually.

What it will take

1. Just over $100 million in additional philanthropic capital over roughly the next eight years, with earlier commitments enabling faster scaling. We estimate that getting from here to around one billion people reached annually and commercial break-even will require just over $100 million in additional philanthropic capital. This would fund country expansion, manufacturing capacity, R&D, evidence generation and the organisational investments needed to support that growth. Earlier commitments could allow us to enter countries in parallel, build manufacturing capacity sooner, strengthen evidence and research, and recruit key teams earlier — ultimately getting micronutrients to more people who need them sooner.

We have already seen how large, flexible capital can change Sanku’s growth trajectory. In 2021, MacKenzie Scott gave Sanku an unrestricted $8 million grant, at a time when our annual budget was around $2 million. We used it to expand into Kenya and Ethiopia, strengthen leadership and operations, and build Eastern Africa’s first dedicated nutrient premix factory in Tanzania.

2. Organisational capacity to support expansion into more countries. Expanding into several more countries will require another step-change in Sanku’s organisational capacity.  Priorities include recruitment and People Ops, country and regional leadership, finance and information systems, manufacturing management, and research and M&E. We are already investing in these areas so that our teams and systems can keep pace with expansion.

How you can help Sanku scale

Advice and collaboration. We would value input from people with experience scaling high-impact organisations, particularly on country expansion and prioritisation, evidence and M&E, organisational design, recruitment and People Ops, manufacturing and supply chains. Introductions to people or organisations with relevant expertise would also be very helpful.

Funding: Our near-term funding picture has two parts:

  • Around $7 million to close the FY27 funding gap. Our approved FY27 plan assumes around $13 million in philanthropic funding, of which approximately $6 million has been secured.
  • Roughly $8 million in additional room for more funding. Beyond the approved FY27 plan, we have identified projects and workstreams that could begin in FY27 if further funding were available, including the planned switch to NaFeEDTA for small maize mills in Tanzania, accelerated country expansion, manufacturing, evidence generation, and building the team, recruitment and People Ops capacity needed to scale effectively.
  • You can donate to Sanku via Every.org. Tax-effective giving options are also available through The Life You Can Save in Australia and the UK, Rethink Charity in Canada and High Impact Athletes in New Zealand. For more information about ways to give, visit sanku.com/donate

People. We expect to recruit significantly as Sanku grows, including across country and regional leadership, research and M&E, manufacturing and other enabling functions. If you might be interested in working with Sanku in future, or know people we should speak to, we would be glad to hear from you.

See the work first-hand. We welcome people interested in visiting Sanku’s work in East Africa, including partner mills and our premix factories in Tanzania and Ethiopia.

Contact: Felix Brooks-church, Co-Founder & CEO (fbrookschurch@sanku.com), or Rickard Vikström, Senior Advisor to CEO (rvikstrom@sanku.com).

Rickard also serves on the board of The Life You Can Save Australia, which recommends Sanku. He is not involved in decisions about which organisations The Life You Can Save recommends.

Based on our current projections, this measure falls from about $0.06 in FY27 to $0.02 in FY30. Commercial revenue, which covered around one-third of operating costs in FY26, is one reason the donor subsidy falls as Sanku scales. Sanku’s early work focused on making fortification practical in those mills.

Sanku invented the Dosifier to make fortification practical in these smaller mills. The Dosifier is a patented, IoT-enabled machine fitted directly to milling equipment, with nearly 1,800 units now deployed. It automatically adds a precise amount of nutrient premix as flour is produced and can transmit operating data through a cellular connection, allowing Sanku to monitor use remotely and identify when a mill needs maintenance, restocking or support.

One of our earliest scaling lessons was that the technology was only one part of making fortification work reliably. Working directly with millers made clear that consistent fortification also depended on reliable premix supply, training, maintenance, quality assurance, field support and an enabling regulatory environment. Sanku gradually built these capabilities around the Dosifier, including supply chains, field teams, monitoring systems, commercial operations and government partnerships.

Building local nutrient premix production was one of the most important additions to Sanku’s model. Sanku built and operates Eastern Africa’s first dedicated nutrient premix factory in Tanzania, which opened in 2024. Before this, millers depended heavily on imported premix, with high costs, long lead times and greater supply risk. Local production has significantly reduced costs and lead times while giving Sanku greater control over quality and supply. A second factory in Addis Ababa has now been completed and premix production will officially start in November this year.

Sanku now works across the milling sector, from last-mile village mills to large producers. The small and medium mills Sanku was created to reach remain central to the model, but larger producers can reach millions of people and use the same nutrient-production, supply-chain and quality assurance (QA) infrastructure. Working across the sector has contributed substantially to Sanku’s recent growth and commercial revenue.

Working with larger mills also makes additionality harder to estimate. At many small mills, RP assumes fortification without Sanku is negligible. Large mills are more likely to fortify to some degree anyway, and the available evidence on what would happen without Sanku is limited. Our reach figure therefore measures the number of people estimated to consume flour fortified through Sanku-supported systems; it is not itself a measure of counterfactual impact. We return to this below because improving the evidence on this question is now one of our priorities.

Three lessons from scaling across Tanzania, Kenya and Ethiopia

Scaling across Tanzania, Kenya and Ethiopia has given us a clearer view of what it takes to grow effectively. Three lessons in particular are shaping our next phase.

1. Build with millers, and adapt to the market

Working directly with millers has shaped both our technology and our wider operating model. More than 500 millers were involved in the R&D and field testing of the Dosifier, providing feedback based on real operating conditions. In Tanzania, millers told us that reducing what they spent on flour bags would make it easier to absorb the cost of fortification. Sanku now produces and sells millions of bags each month, with the commercial margin helping offset the cost of premix.

Local market conditions also shape which parts of the model work in each country. We initially expected the bag model to work in Kenya too, but it did not prove viable there. It is currently used only in Tanzania, although we think it may be well suited to Uganda. Our approach is therefore to take the underlying capabilities — technology, nutrient production, QA, monitoring, supply chains and field operations — into new countries while adapting how they are deployed locally.

2. Establish stronger baselines before entering new markets

Stronger baseline data should improve both how we design new-country work and how credibly we estimate its additional impact. In Kenya and Ethiopia, we did not establish as strong a baseline before scaling as we would now want, which makes it harder to estimate retrospectively what would have happened without Sanku. This is particularly important when working with larger mills, where some fortification may already be happening. Before entering new markets, we now want a clearer picture of existing fortification and compliance, the structure of the milling sector and the main implementation gaps. The RP work discussed below reinforced the importance of doing this earlier.

3. Recruitment and People Ops can become a constraint on scale

Our experience aligns with two recent arguments about absorptive capacity: Jack Lewars’s Donors should push animal welfare and global health charities to have more robust scaling plans and Berke Çelik and Tony Senanayake’s People Operations Gap in Global Health. Both argue, in different ways, that scaling effectively requires investing in management, recruitment and people systems before they become bottlenecks.

As Sanku expanded from one country to three, recruitment and People Ops sometimes constrained how quickly we could build the teams we needed. Limited funding certainty has also sometimes made it harder to recruit continuously and move quickly when particularly strong candidates became available. For the next phase, we want to invest more now in recruitment and People Ops, alongside leadership and other enabling functions, so that we can hire, develop and retain the people needed to scale effectively.

What we learned from the Rethink Priorities analysis — and how we’re acting on it

Alongside what we had learned from scaling, we wanted an independent cost-effectiveness analysis to identify where our current work could improve, understand the most important evidence gaps and uncertainties, and better inform future country expansion. We therefore commissioned and funded Rethink Priorities (RP) to analyse our work in Tanzania, Kenya and Ethiopia. RP is responsible for the report and its conclusions. The full report is available here.

RP estimates substantial differences in impact and cost-effectiveness across the three countries covered by the analysis. It reports its cost-per-DALY estimates both gross of revenue and net of revenue; in the net figures, revenue from Sanku’s commercial sales is used to offset programme costs.

RP’s multiple of GiveWell’s benchmark combines its modelled health and economic benefits. See the full report for the methodology and assumptions.

The difference between the gross and net figures also shows the role of Sanku’s commercial model: revenue from miller sales reduces the philanthropic cost of generating a given level of modelled impact. All else equal, as commercial revenue covers a larger share of operating costs over time, the net-of-revenue cost per DALY should fall further.

Part of the difference across countries reflects the maturity and scale of Sanku’s operations. RP says Tanzania’s stronger result reflects “both the maturity and scale of the Tanzanian operation” as well as its relatively low-compliance environment. Tanzania is our oldest and largest operation, while Kenya and Ethiopia are newer markets that have not yet reached the same scale. RP’s cost analysis also finds that fixed country-presence costs are particularly important at low operating scale. These factors are only part of the explanation, however; country context and counterfactual assumptions also have a major effect on the results.

Tanzania has the strongest results. RP estimates Tanzania at ~4.6× GiveWell’s benchmark today, which it describes as “commendably close” to GiveWell’s current 6× funding bar. It estimates ~8.2× if all Sanku-supported flour in Tanzania switched to using the iron compound NaFeEDTA, which would put Tanzania above that bar. We plan to make the switch only for our small maize mills, and subject to securing the necessary funding, so the full 8.2× should be read as an upper bound rather than an estimate of the planned transition.

Kenya and Ethiopia score lower for different reasons. In Kenya, much of Sanku’s work is with industrial-scale mills, which RP assumes would already fortify to some degree without Sanku. That assumed counterfactual fortification comes with substantial uncertainty, and RP says cost-effectiveness would be significantly higher under plausible alternative values. RP also models a higher-counterfactual scenario in which these estimates fall substantially. In Ethiopia, the national fortification standard excludes iron. Iron accounts for more than 90% of the DALYs RP estimates Sanku averts in Tanzania and Kenya, and all of RP’s modelled economic-benefit channels are linked to iron. Ethiopia therefore has no modelled wage gains. At the same time, commercial revenue reduces Ethiopia’s estimated cost per DALY from $1,918 gross to $617 net of revenue, and RP notes that its revenue model may be particularly sustainable.

There is substantial uncertainty around the estimates, and RP notes that its assumptions may “either upwardly or downwardly bias our headline results”. It identifies three particularly important uncertainties: counterfactual fortification, the estimated effects of fortification on relative risks for key health outcomes, and the assumption of a linear dose-response relationship between nutrient intake and health impacts.

For example, one potential upward bias is the assumption that any additional malaria risk from increased iron intake is negligible. RP notes that the evidence is mixed and cites a 2026 Cochrane review finding little to no effect of iron supplementation on clinical malaria overall. Given the relatively low malaria prevalence in the three countries analysed, RP does not model this effect, but notes that this may slightly overstate estimated health benefits. In the other direction, the report excludes possible indirect effects from Sanku’s work on fortification among non-partner mills, which may bias its estimate of total benefits downwards.

How we’re acting on the findings

  • Switching Tanzania’s small maize mills back to NaFeEDTA, subject to funding. The iron compound we use today fully meets Tanzania’s national fortification standard and continues to deliver meaningful health benefits. But RP’s analysis finds that switching to the more bioavailable NaFeEDTA could increase those benefits substantially and improve cost-effectiveness. We used NaFeEDTA previously and stepped back from it following stockouts, logistical challenges and cost pressures. We are targeting small maize mills because maize’s higher phytate content makes the benefit of the more bioavailable iron compound particularly important there, and because the switch is operationally feasible for these mills; large wheat mills are not currently a practical target. Subject to securing funding for the additional cost, we plan to make the switch.
  • Improving baseline data before entering new markets. As discussed above, we want a clearer picture of existing fortification and compliance before scaling, particularly where larger mills may already be fortifying to some degree but the quality and consistency of that fortification are uncertain. This should help us design around the actual implementation gaps and estimate our counterfactual impact more credibly, while also giving us a better basis for assessing any indirect impact on fortification beyond Sanku partner mills.
  • Sharpening how cost-effectiveness informs expansion decisions. Cost-effectiveness is already an important input into how we assess opportunities to scale. The RP analysis gives us a stronger basis for using it alongside evidence, operational feasibility and country context when deciding where and how to expand.

Why scale further, and what it will take

Micronutrient deficiencies remain a major global health burden, while many countries still lack the infrastructure and systems needed to fortify staple foods reliably at scale. Uganda is now Sanku’s fourth country, with operations just getting underway. Over roughly the next decade, we aim to grow to around ten countries and reach approximately one billion people annually.

What it will take

1. Just over $100 million in additional philanthropic capital over roughly the next eight years, with earlier commitments enabling faster scaling. We estimate that getting from here to around one billion people reached annually and commercial break-even will require just over $100 million in additional philanthropic capital. This would fund country expansion, manufacturing capacity, R&D, evidence generation and the organisational investments needed to support that growth. Earlier commitments could allow us to enter countries in parallel, build manufacturing capacity sooner, strengthen evidence and research, and recruit key teams earlier — ultimately getting micronutrients to more people who need them sooner.

We have already seen how large, flexible capital can change Sanku’s growth trajectory. In 2021, MacKenzie Scott gave Sanku an unrestricted $8 million grant, at a time when our annual budget was around $2 million. We used it to expand into Kenya and Ethiopia, strengthen leadership and operations, and build Eastern Africa’s first dedicated nutrient premix factory in Tanzania.

2. Organisational capacity to support expansion into more countries. Expanding into several more countries will require another step-change in Sanku’s organisational capacity.  Priorities include recruitment and People Ops, country and regional leadership, finance and information systems, manufacturing management, and research and M&E. We are already investing in these areas so that our teams and systems can keep pace with expansion.

Advice and collaboration. We would value input from people with experience scaling high-impact organisations, particularly on country expansion and prioritisation, evidence and M&E, organisational design, recruitment and People Ops, manufacturing and supply chains. People. We expect to recruit significantly as Sanku grows, including across country and regional leadership, research and M&E, manufacturing and other enabling functions. If you might be interested in working with Sanku in future, or know people we should speak to, we would be glad to hear from you.

See the work first-hand. We welcome people interested in visiting Sanku’s work in East Africa, including partner mills and our premix factories in Tanzania and Ethiopia.
